topic: Zone 2 training for endurance athletes: physiological rationale, how intensity is defined and what the research evidence shows

key_points.point: Zone 2 has no single standard definition: it is usually the intensity at or below the first lactate/ventilatory threshold (LT1/VT1), about 2 mmol/L lactate or lower, often approximated at roughly 68-75% of max heart rate.

Terminology and zone models differ (three-zone vs five-zone; 'anaerobic threshold' used for both VT1 and VT2); percent-HRmax, %VO2max or MET prescriptions ignore individual variability, so threshold-anchored intensity is preferred.

Rationale: San-Millan and Brooks found fat oxidation inversely related to blood lactate across athletes, moderately active people and metabolic syndrome, proposing both as indirect markers of mitochondrial function and metabolic flexibility; evidence is correlational.

Mechanistic caveat: training volume appears the main driver of mitochondrial content, while intensity (high-intensity intervals at 90% or more of maximal aerobic power) drives gains in mitochondrial respiratory function.
Descriptive studies of elite endurance athletes show about 80% of sessions at low intensity (around 2 mmol/L lactate) and about 20% high intensity, which motivates the polarized/zone-2-heavy model.

A 2025 individual-participant network meta-analysis (13 studies, 348 athletes) found no difference between polarized and pyramidal training for VO2max (SMD -0.06) or time-trial performance (SMD -0.05).

Evidence limitations: interventions lasted only 3-18 weeks, several studies had high risk of bias or were non-randomized, women were about 15% of participants, and intensity was classified from heart-rate time-in-zone.

Interval training counterpoint: HIIT and sprint interval training improve aerobic fitness and mitochondrial content similarly to moderate continuous training; at matched volume HIIT tends to raise VO2max more.

Subgroup results suggest competitive athletes may gain more VO2max from polarized and recreational athletes from pyramidal training (SMD -0.63 between subgroups), but this is confounded by baseline fitness and is hypothesis-generating.
Practical criticism: lactate thresholds can vary day to day, so fixed lactate or heart-rate zone numbers may be imprecise; lab testing is costly. This is an expert opinion piece, not a trial.
Seiler's review noted that adding more high-intensity interval work to already well-trained athletes did not convincingly yield long-term performance gains.
